If you had consulted Nitin, he would have ________ you.
questions.solution:
The most appropriate option to fill in the blank is: a) advised

The sentence would read: "If you had consulted Nitin, he would have advised you."

The format of the sentence is a conditional sentence using the third conditional pattern. The third conditional is used to express a hypothetical situation in the past and the hypothetical result that would have occurred if the situation had been different. The format is as follows:

"If + past perfect (had + past participle), + subject + would/could/might + have + past participle."

In the given sentence: "If you had consulted Nitin, he would have advised you."

"If you had consulted Nitin" represents the past hypothetical situation.

"He would have advised you" represents the hypothetical result that would have occurred.

questions.question: Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow. In 1998, one of us, Daniel Goleman, published his first article on emotional intelligence and leadership. The response to “What Makes a Leader?” was enthusiastic. People throughout and beyond the business community started talking about the vital role that empathy and self-knowledge play in effective leadership. The concept of emotional intelligence continues to occupy a prominent space in the leadership literature and in everyday coaching practices. But in the past five years, research in the emerging field of social neuroscience—the study of what happens in the brain while people interact—is beginning to reveal subtle new truths about what makes a good leader. The salient discovery is that certain things leaders do—specifically, exhibit empathy and become attuned to others’ moods—literally affect both their own brain chemistry and that of their followers. Indeed, researchers have found that the leader-follower dynamic is not a case of two (or more) independent brains reacting consciously or unconsciously to each other. Rather, the individual minds become, in a sense, fused into a single system. We believe that great leaders are those whose behaviour powerfully leverages the system of brain interconnectedness. We place them on the opposite end of the neural continuum from people with serious social disorders, such as autism or Asperger’s syndrome, that are characterized by underdevelopment in the areas of the brain associated with social interactions. If we are correct, it follows that a potent way of becoming a better leader is to find authentic contexts in which to learn the kinds of social behaviour that reinforce the brain’s social circuitry. Leading effectively is, in other words, less about mastering situations—or even mastering social skill sets—than about developing a genuine interest in and talent for fostering positive feelings in the people whose cooperation and support you need. The notion that effective leadership is about having powerful social circuits in the brain has prompted us to extend our concept of emotional intelligence, which we had grounded in theories of individual psychology. A more relationship-based construct for assessing leadership is social intelligence, which we define as a set of interpersonal competencies built on specific neural circuits (and related endocrine systems) that inspire others to be effective. How does the concept of social intelligence differ from emotional intelligence, as presented in the passage?

When her mother was expecting Santosh, a travelling ‘holy man’, giving her his blessing, assumed that she wanted a son. But, to everyone’s surprise, the unborn child’s grandmother, who was standing close by, told him that they did not want a son. The ‘holy man’ was also surprised! Nevertheless, he gave the requested blessing ... and as destiny would have it, the blessing seemed to work. Santosh was born the sixth child in a family with five sons, a sister to five brothers. She was born in the small village of Joniyawas of Rewari District in Haryana. The girl was given the name ‘Santosh’, which means contentment. But Santosh was not always content with her place in a traditional way of life. She began living life on her own terms from the start. Where other girls wore traditional Indian dresses, Santosh preferred shorts. Looking back, she says now, “From the very beginning I was quite determined that if I chose a correct and a rational path, the others around me had to change, not me.” Santosh’s parents were affluent landowners who could afford to send their children to the best schools, even to the country’s capital, New Delhi, which was quite close by. But, in line with the prevailing custom in the family, Santosh had to make do with the local village school. So, she decided to fight the system in her own quiet way when the right moment arrived. And the right moment came when she turned sixteen. At sixteen, most of the girls in her village used to get married. Santosh was also under pressure from her parents to do the same. A marriage as early as that was the last thing on her mind. She threatened her parents that she would never marry if she did not get a proper education. She left home and got herself enrolled in a school in Delhi. When her parents refused to pay for her education, she politely informed them of her plans to earn money by working part time to pay her school fees. Her parents then agreed to pay for her education. What theme is the passage primarily focused on?

Length: The Grand Trunk Road stretches for approximately 2,500 kilometers (1,550 miles) across northern India and into parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh. It runs from Kolkata (formerly Calcutta) in West Bengal, India, to Kabul in Afghanistan, passing through several major cities and towns.

questions.question: In which part of the circulatory system does the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide occur with body tissues?
questions.questionHtml: In which part of the circulatory system does the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide occur with body tissues?
questions.solution:
Option C is the correct answer.

The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide with body tissues occurs primarily in the capillaries. Capillaries are the smallest and most numerous blood vessels in the circulatory system, and they are responsible for facilitating the exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products between the bloodstream and the body's cells.

Arteries: Arteries are blood vessels that carry oxygenated blood away from the heart to various parts of the body. They have thick, muscular walls to withstand the high pressure generated by the heart's contractions.

Veins: Veins are blood vessels that return deoxygenated blood from the body's tissues back to the heart. They often have thinner walls than arteries and contain valves to prevent blood from flowing backward.

Atria: The atria are the upper chambers of the heart (right atrium and left atrium). They receive blood returning to the heart and then contract to pump it into the lower chambers (ventricles). The atria play a role in ensuring efficient blood flow through the heart.

Rickets is a disease that primarily affects children and is characterized by the weakening and softening of the bones. It is mainly caused by a deficiency of Vitamin D, which is essential for the proper absorption of calcium and phosphorus in the body.

Role of Vitamin D: Vitamin D is often referred to as the "sunshine vitamin" because the body can produce it when the skin is exposed to sunlight. This vitamin plays a crucial role in maintaining bone health by aiding the absorption of calcium from the diet into the bloodstream. Adequate levels of Vitamin D are necessary for the mineralization and strengthening of bones.

Vitamin D Deficiency: When there is a deficiency of Vitamin D in the body, it can lead to impaired calcium absorption. This, in turn, results in soft and weak bones, which are characteristic of rickets.

Should the Government restrict use of electricity for each household depending upon the requirement?

This argument is strong because it addresses the issue of inadequate electricity generation. If there is a shortage of electricity, it may be necessary for the government to restrict electricity usage to ensure that everyone gets a fair share and that the power grid does not become overloaded.

II. "No, every citizen has the right to consume electricity as per their requirement as they pay for using electricity."

This argument is also strong, as it emphasizes the principle of individual rights and consumer choice. Citizens do pay for their electricity usage, and restricting their usage may infringe on their freedom to use electricity as they see fit. It highlights the importance of respecting individual freedoms and choices.

III. "No, the government does not have the machinery to put such a restriction on the use of electricity."

This argument is not strong because it suggests that the government lacks the capability to enforce restrictions on electricity usage. However, the government often has the regulatory authority and infrastructure in place to monitor and control various aspects of utility services, including electricity. Whether or not they have the machinery to implement such restrictions would depend on the specific context and government capabilities.

Considering the strength of each argument, the correct answer is:
